scenarios.title: Typical department
scenarios.description: A department as one actually is: comfortable but not idle (80 % of the annual ceiling planned), a handful of qualified candidates per discipline, ceilings on most staff and floors on some. The reference point every other scenario is read against.

scenarios.title: No individual constraints
scenarios.description: Identical structure to the baseline, but no lecturer carries a constraint of their own — only the university-wide default ceiling applies. Isolates the cost the search pays for merely having slots and candidates, with every feasibility check trivially satisfied. The control.

scenarios.title: Tight ceilings, no floors
scenarios.description: Every lecturer carries an hour ceiling close to what they will actually be given, plus distinct-course ceilings of every family. Nobody has a floor, so the repair pass has nothing to do and the whole cost lands on the greedy feasibility scan.

scenarios.title: Floors on most staff
scenarios.description: The mirror image: generous ceilings, but most lecturers must reach a minimum number of hours and of distinct courses by type. The greedy alone cannot satisfy a floor — it can only fill slots — so this is the scenario in which the repair pass does real work.

scenarios.title: Two or three candidates per discipline
scenarios.description: The narrow-expertise department: each discipline has only two or three people who can teach it. Feasible pools are tiny, so most-constrained-first ordering decides almost everything and the improvement pass has nowhere to move to.

scenarios.title: Broad interchangeability
scenarios.description: The opposite of the previous one: a dozen people are qualified for each discipline, as at a large general-education department. Every feasibility scan walks a long list, and the improvement pass has many better candidates to try. The worst case for the candidate loop.

scenarios.title: Filling gaps in an existing plan
scenarios.description: Half the positions already have their lecturers and are locked; the run only fills what is missing. This is the common case in practice — a department revisits its plan in September — and it is the one where locked assignments consume capacity that the repair and improvement passes are then forbidden to reclaim.

scenarios.title: More work than the department can hold
scenarios.description: Planned hours exceed the annual capacity of the whole department by about a third, with tight ceilings on top. Provably infeasible: the correct behaviour is to fill what can be filled and report the rest. Included because the failure path is the one an algorithm is most likely to spend unbounded time in, and a paper should show it does not.
